full_judgment: 16. We may observe that there are several reported decisions on this section. The preponderance of opinion is in substance of what we have expressed above. Of the reported decisions may be mentioned: Makhan Lal Saha Vs. The Crown, (1950) 2 DLR 223, and Sachi Nanda Kunda Vs. The Crown (1955) 7 DLR 216. In both the decisions, the accused was required to be a witness in the case, and in consideration of that, consent was granted. The decision says the grounds need not be recorded by the Magistrate, if there is material on record to reveal the ground of withdrawal. Superintendent, Legal Affairs Vs. Azizul Huq, (1960) 12 DLR 324 also says that the assigning of reason is not essential for allowing withdrawal. In State Vs. Eusubali (1968) 20 DLR 518, it has been held that allowing the prayer for withdrawal is not a matter of course, but involves the exercise of judicial discretion. The direction of Addl. Superintendent of Police to withdraw without disclosing the ground was held not to be a good ground to give consent to withdraw. We like to refer to two latest decisions of the High Court Division Abdur Rab Vs. Syed Ahmed (1974) 26 DLR 133, and (2) Govinda Shed Jamadar Vs. State (1975) 27 DLR 67. In both cases a large number of decisions have been considered and the law enunciated. In the case of Abdur Rah the withdrawal was sought by the Court Sub-Inspector upon a direction of the Superintendent of Police and the opinion of the public Prosecutor, and it was allowed by the Magistrate without ass signing any reason. It was held that the materials disclosed before the court did not reveal any reasonable ground for grant of consent to the withdrawal of the Prosecution. In the case of Govinda Shed withdrawal was sought by the public prosecutor with a copy of the Government order, which disclosed that the Government had decided to withdraw the case of collaboration against the accused. The order of withdrawal though without any reason was upheld upon the consideration that the decision was arrived at by the Ministry of Home Affairs, a high administrative authority of the Government, and the disclosure of decision of such a high authority is itself a good ground for withdrawal.
